title: React components, patterns and hooks
tagline: Lifecycle, lifting state, context, HOCs, render props, and the hooks that replaced most of them.
intro: Class components are rare in new code but everywhere in old code, and every hook is easier to understand once you know which class feature it replaced.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: A component's life, and the hook for each part of it.

blocks.caption: Mount once, update many times, unmount once.

items.label: Mounting
items.detail: The view is created and added to the tree; runs exactly once per instance
explain: In a class: constructor, render, then componentDidMount. The constructor must call super(props) before it may touch this.
With hooks: the function body renders, then useEffect(fn, []) runs once after the first paint — the same moment as componentDidMount.
That is the place for a fetch or a subscription. A timer started here is the one you must stop at unmount.

items.label: Updating
items.detail: New props or state re-render the view; runs as many times as they change
explain: In a class, componentDidUpdate(prevProps, prevState) runs after each update, and you compare old with new yourself.
useEffect(fn, [a, b]) does the comparison for you: it reruns only when a or b changed since the last render.

items.label: Unmounting
items.detail: The view leaves the tree; the last chance to cancel timers and subscriptions
explain: In a class this is componentWillUnmount. With hooks, it is the function returned from useEffect.
Forget it and a setInterval keeps calling setState on a component that no longer exists, which leaks and warns.

sections.title: Lifting state
sections.summary: The parent owns the state; the child asks it to change.

items: The parent passes a function down as a prop.
The child calls it on a click or a toggle.
The function sets the parent's state, and both re-render.

blocks.caption: In a class, the method loses this unless it is bound or wrapped
code: // …or wrap in an arrow function where it is passed

sections.title: Context
sections.summary: Data for a whole subtree, without passing props level by level.

items: A Provider wraps the subtree and holds the value.
Class components read it with a Consumer; function components with useContext.
Providers nest, so a theme context and a user context can sit one inside the other.

blocks.caption: useContext: no Consumer, no render function
code: return <button style={{ background: theme.background, color: theme.foreground }}>Themed</button>;

body: Every consumer re-renders when the value changes. Keep fast-changing data out of a context that half the app reads.

sections.title: HOCs and render props
sections.summary: The two class-era ways to share logic.

rows: A function that takes a component and returns a new one with extra behaviour
A prop that is a function, telling the component what to render

blocks.caption: A HOC; the wrapped component's name must start with a capital letter
Render props: the parent decides the markup, Counter owns the state

items: Call hooks at the top level only — never inside a loop, a condition or a nested function.
Call them only from function components or from custom hooks.
React matches hooks to state by call order, which is why the order must be the same on every render.

sections.title: useMemo and useCallback
sections.summary: Skip work that the last render already did.

blocks.caption: Why an unrelated click was slow, and the fix.

items.label: Any state changes
items.detail: Clicking 'change key' updates key, and the whole component function runs again
explain: A re-render calls every line of the function body. An expensive call written there runs again, even if its input did not change.
In the example, a loop building a 5,000,000-item array logs 'called with input: 3' on every click of an unrelated button.

items.label: useMemo
items.detail: Keeps the last result and recomputes only when a dependency changes
explain: useMemo(() => expensive(num), [num]) runs once on mount and again only when num changes; clicking 'change key' no longer logs.
It returns a value. Use it for derived data that is costly to build, not for every calculation — the bookkeeping has a cost too.

items.label: useCallback
items.detail: Keeps the same function object between renders until a dependency changes
explain: useCallback(fn, deps) is useMemo(() => fn, deps). It returns a function, not the result of calling one.
It matters when the function is passed to a memoised child or used as an effect dependency, where a new identity would re-render or re-run it.

sections.title: useRef
sections.summary: A box that survives re-renders without causing one.

items: useRef(initial) returns { current: initial }, and the same object for the component's whole life.
Attach it to an element with ref={…} to reach the mounted node, e.g. to focus an input.
Writing to ref.current does not re-render — use it for values the screen does not show, such as a timer id.
